metadata.title: Is reading contagious? Examining parents’ and children’s reading attitudes and behaviors

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This policy brief uses PIRLS 2011 background data from student and parent questionnaires for 4th-grade students across 50 education systems. The analytic focus is on binary/dichotomized questionnaire outcomes (enjoy reading; read frequently) and their co-occurrence between parents and children, with reading achievement used only as contextual information. The brief does not report whether PIRLS sampling weights or replicate-weight procedures were applied, nor does it name any weight variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT) or replicate design (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Because the analysis is descriptive and correlational (no ML modeling is reported), the manuscript provides insufficient information to determine whether complex survey weighting was used.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible values are not applicable because the dependent variables analyzed in the brief are questionnaire-based reading attitudes and behaviors (e.g., agreement with “I enjoy reading” and frequency categories for reading for fun), not PIRLS achievement scores modeled via PVs. The brief also does not describe any missing-data strategy for questionnaire responses (e.g., complete-case selection or imputation), representing a reporting gap for transparency.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PIRLS 2011 4th-grade student and parent questionnaire data from education systems that administered both the student and parent questionnaires. The brief reports that three additional education systems participated in PIRLS 2011 but did not administer the parent questionnaire and therefore were not included: England, the United States, and Florida (USA). The outcomes analyzed are dichotomized reading enjoyment (agreed a lot vs disagreed a little/a lot with “I enjoy reading”) and reading frequency (every day/almost every day vs never/almost never for reading for enjoyment at home / reading for fun outside of school).

data.outcome_summary: This IEA policy brief uses PIRLS 2011 Grade 4 student and parent questionnaire data from 50 education systems (about 270,000 students) to examine whether parents’ positive reading attitudes and behaviors are “contagious.” The outcomes are dichotomized reading enjoyment (“I enjoy reading” agreed a lot) and reading frequency (every day/almost every day vs never/almost never). Across most systems, higher shares of both parents and children report enjoying reading and reading frequently, and children’s positive responses are more common when parents also report positive attitudes/behaviors (e.g., on average about two-thirds vs about half for enjoyment; about half vs about one-third for reading frequently). The brief further reports that girls are more likely than boys to enjoy and read frequently when parents are positive, while differences by parents’ education are weaker and less consistent. The analysis is correlational and does not support causal claims; the brief also does not report missing-data handling or any survey-weighting details.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This extraction targets an official assessment framework, user guide, or technical manual without an empirical ML study. Sample sizes, ML algorithms, and predictive findings are intentionally null or empty per schema rules for non-empirical IEA/OECD documentation.
